metadata.file_name: 76. Guo et al. (2024). Human-Centered AI for Discovering Student Engagement Profiles on Large-Scale Educational Assessments.pdf
metadata.title: Human-Centered AI for Discovering Student Engagement Profiles on Large-Scale Educational Assessments
metadata.venue: Journal of Measurement and Evaluation in Education and Psychology

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses NAEP Grade 8 Mathematics digital assessment process/log data for a single NAEP item block (2022 administration; 14 items; 30 minutes). The manuscript reports a final analytic sample size after excluding students with irregular response time and abnormal completion, but it does not describe the application of NAEP complex survey weights or any replicate-weight procedure. Because the paper focuses on ML-based profile discovery and active learning with deep learning (autoencoder + LSTM) and supervised ensemble classification (random forest + SVC), it does not report a weighting variable (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or how weights were incorporated into model training or evaluation. As a result, readers should treat the reported profile proportions and model behavior as conditional on the analytic sample rather than explicitly population-representative estimates.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables in this study are engagement profile labels derived from process/log-derived features (navigation sequences, response-time categories, and derived test-level aggregates) rather than NAEP cognitive achievement scores with plausible values. The paper does not describe any missing-data strategy for questionnaire/background variables or for process-log features (e.g., how missing timestamps, tool-use logs, or incomplete sequences were handled beyond excluding irregular response time/abnormal completion). This is a reporting gap because process-log datasets commonly contain partial or missing events that can affect sequence modeling and clustering.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used NAEP 2022 Grade 8 Mathematics digital assessment process/log data for one publicly released item block containing 14 items (30 minutes). Excluded students with irregular response time and abnormal completion on the selected item block; the remaining analytic sample size is N=14,008.

main_findings.dataset_used: NAEP 2022 Grade 8 Mathematics (digital) — one released item block (14 items)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Not reported (profile frequencies reported; model accuracy/confidence thresholds described but no numeric accuracy metrics provided). Additional analysis (Engagement profile membership (fully labeled profiles after active learning)): Not reported (stopping rule based on inability to improve model accuracy; pseudo-label confidence threshold >0.75 used).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using NAEP 2022 Grade 8 Mathematics digital item-block the study leveraged total score, total response time, total number of visits, item response-time categories, and item navigation sequences to create engagement profiles, finding ten differentiable profiles with more than half associated with low-performing students. This indicates that combining process/log-derived timing and navigation context with performance information can produce actionable, human-interpretable engagement typologies for low-achieving learners, though the paper does not report predictive accuracy metrics for the profile classifier.

data.outcome_summary: The study demonstrates a human-centered AI (HAI) framework using NAEP 2022 Grade 8 Mathematics digital process/log data from one released item block (14 items; 30 minutes). After excluding students with irregular response time and abnormal completion, the analytic sample contains 14,008 students from the USA. Step 1 created interpretable process features, including item response-time categories derived from item-specific rapid-responding thresholds and test-level aggregates (total score, total response time, total visits). Step 2 used an autoencoder with LSTM layers to compress sequential navigation information into an 8-dimensional latent space, then clustered students (K-means with 30 clusters) and had human experts label representative and extreme cases, yielding 10 engagement profiles with more than half linked to low-performing students. Step 3 scaled labeling via active learning with a soft-voting ensemble (random forest + SVC), using pseudo-label confidence thresholds (e.g., >0.75), but the paper does not report numeric predictive metrics or survey-weighted estimates, limiting claims about population representativeness and classifier accuracy.
